title: Syncboard: a local-first collaborative kanban board
tagline: Operation-log state, CRDT-style merge, offline conflict review and time travel, all hand-built and runnable in two browser tabs.
summary: I built a Trello-style kanban board whose entire state is an append-only log of immutable ops that a pure reducer folds into the board. Open it in two windows and edits sync live; flip the offline switch and your changes queue while simulated teammates keep working, then reconnect to review genuine conflicts. A guided tour that auto-completes from real events walks a visitor through all of it.
highlights: I designed the state model as an operation log (id, lamport clock, author, timestamp) with last-writer-wins registers per field and fractional-index ordering, so applying ops is commutative and idempotent; unit tests shuffle concurrent ops 30 times and assert identical boards.

I hand-built drag and drop on pointer events with a drop placeholder, edge auto-scroll, long-press touch support and a full keyboard path (Space, arrows, Esc) with aria-live announcements, using no DnD library.

I implemented real multi-tab sync over BroadcastChannel with localStorage persistence, per-tab offline queues, and a Conflict Review panel with word-level diffs and keep-mine / keep-theirs / merge resolutions that are written back as new ops.
I made undo and redo operate through the log as inverse ops scoped to my own actions, and built a time-travel scrubber whose 'restore this version' appends diff ops instead of rewriting history.

I wrote a guided tour whose eight steps complete only when the matching real op or event fires, and a Playwright script that performs it across two pages (including CDP touch drag) and asserts every step.
I kept the engine framework-agnostic and strictly typed (core/ has no React), with a command palette, shortcuts sheet, light/dark theme, reduced-motion support and phone-width snap scrolling.

title: Pulse: live observability and incident console
tagline: A Datadog-style console with a hand-built Canvas chart engine and query language, running on a simulated backend in a Web Worker.
summary: I built a browser-only observability console: live-streaming metrics, a 240k-line log explorer with its own query language, alert rules, and a full incident workflow. Everything runs on a seeded simulator in a Web Worker, and a guided mission lets visitors investigate a planted outage end to end. I wrote the chart renderer and the query engine from scratch, with no charting or UI libraries.
highlights: I hand-built a Canvas 2D time-series renderer: min/max pixel-bucket decimation that provably preserves spikes, a two-layer canvas, DPR-correct sizing, off-screen skipping and a single rAF loop that only runs when something is dirty.

I implemented linked interaction across charts: brush-to-zoom, shift-drag pan, cursor-anchored wheel zoom, keyboard time navigation, a crosshair and tooltip synchronised across every chart, deploy markers and threshold lines.

I wrote a log query language from scratch (tokenizer, recursive-descent parser, compiler to typed-column predicates) with positioned syntax and semantic errors, syntax highlighting, autocomplete, saved queries and filter chips, and a hand-windowed list over 240k rows.

I put the simulation in a Web Worker behind a typed message protocol: seeded generators for 64 metric series and 240k logs, injected incidents (bad deploy, error burst, memory leak), live alert evaluation, and rollbacks that make the metrics actually recover.
I built the incident workflow: declare from an alert, auto-attached timeline of alerts, deploys and notes, status steps, runbook, rollback, and a post-mortem summary generated from measured data.

I built a self-checking guided mission whose steps are detected from real application state, and verified it with 30 unit tests plus a 35-check real-Chrome end-to-end script driven by mouse and keyboard.

title: flowgraph: a workflow editor with a step-through debugger
tagline: Wire nodes into an automation, then watch it run: packets on edges, breakpoints, step into loops, and replayable run history.
summary: I built a Zapier/n8n-style workflow editor from scratch: an infinite SVG and HTML canvas, typed ports, an inspector generated from node schemas, and a pure execution engine with branching, loops, merge, retries and error edges. A debugger runs on top of that engine, with breakpoints, step over and step into, node input and output diffs against the previous run, a Gantt timeline and a scrubbable replay. A guided tour that completes as the visitor performs each step opens on a nearly finished workflow.
highlights: I wrote the execution engine as a pure, event-emitting dataflow scheduler on an injectable clock: edges resolve as live or dead, so branches, Merge, loops with nested regions, exponential-backoff retries, per-node timeouts, error edges and cancellation all fall out of one rule, and a FakeClock makes 12-second workflows deterministic in milliseconds.

I built the debugger as a gate in that engine: breakpoints, pause, step over (a Loop is one step) and step into (pauses inside each iteration). One reducer, deriveView(events, t), drives the live canvas, the Gantt timeline and replay scrubbing, so a past run can be replayed exactly.

I hand-built the canvas without a graph library: cursor-anchored wheel zoom, pinch, trackpad pan, marquee and group move, port-to-port dragging with live bezier preview that lights up valid targets and explains invalid drops, reconnectable edge ends, cycle detection, minimap, and a layered DAG auto-layout (barycenter ordering) that tests show never overlaps nodes.

I wrote an expression language (Pratt parser, pipes, lambdas, safe built-ins, {{ }} templates) with positioned errors, plus a dry-run schema inference pass so the inspector autocompletes variables from upstream data and shows a live preview of a Transform against real or sample data.

Every edit is a command with a computed inverse (undo/redo with coalescing), the graph autosaves, exports to JSON and shares as a deflate-compressed URL hash, and 64 Vitest tests cover the engine, expressions, ports, layout, undo/redo and share round-trip.

I made the guided tour self-completing: eight steps detect whether the visitor actually dragged, wired, edited, ran, broke and inspected, each with a Do it for me button, and verified with a Playwright script that performs them with real mouse drags; keyboard connect mode, ARIA live run announcements and a read-only phone view cover accessibility and small screens.

title: Clinic Desk — front-desk app for small clinics
tagline: A receptionist-first PWA for queues, bookings, billing and follow-ups, built for clinics in Kolkata.
summary: An offline-first React app I built to replace paper, WhatsApp threads and memory at independent clinics. It handles walk-ins and booked slots in one live queue, itemised billing, follow-up tracking and a doctor consult view, in English, Bengali and Hindi.
highlights: I put one data-provider interface in front of two backends: an offline-first Dexie (IndexedDB) provider for single-device use and a Supabase provider for multi-tenant use. Pages never import a database directly, so switching backend is an environment flag.
Clinical notes are encrypted in the browser with AES-GCM using a PBKDF2-derived key (210,000 iterations), so stored records are ciphertext.
A single live queue merges phone, WhatsApp and walk-in patients. Tokens are issued at billing time and never renumbered, while booked slots keep the pre-queue list in time order.
Slot booking respects each doctor's visiting hours, working days and breaks, and records when a patient wanted a slot but none was free, which feeds the analytics view.
A WhatsApp booking bot and notifications run as Netlify functions, with a public booking page and consent captured for each patient.
It is an installable PWA with role-aware screens for front desk and doctors, a mobile bottom-nav layout, and English, Bengali and Hindi UI strings.

title: Clinic Protocol Assistant — retrieval-augmented Q&A
tagline: Ask a question about clinic protocols and get a cited answer. Hybrid keyword and vector retrieval runs entirely in the browser.
summary: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app for clinic staff. It chunks six protocol documents, embeds them in the browser, retrieves with BM25 and vector search merged by reciprocal rank fusion, and asks Claude to answer using only the retrieved passages, citing each one. Without an API key it falls back to extracted, cited sentences. I wrote the documents and an 18-question evaluation set so retrieval quality is measured, not assumed.
highlights: Documents are chunked along their headings (long sections split on sentence boundaries with one sentence of overlap), and the heading stays in the chunk text because it often carries the topic the body never repeats.

Retrieval is hybrid: a from-scratch BM25 index for exact terms and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings (Transformers.js, running in a Web Worker) for meaning, merged with reciprocal rank fusion because the two score scales are not comparable.
Each source card shows its rank in the keyword and meaning searches, so you can see why a passage was chosen, and can switch between Hybrid, Keyword and Meaning to compare.

Generation uses the Claude Messages API streamed straight from the browser with the visitor's own key, held in session storage and sent only to api.anthropic.com. The prompt allows answers only from numbered excerpts, requires [n] citations and tells the model to say when the answer is not in the documents.
Citation markers are only turned into links when they point at an excerpt that was actually sent, so a made-up [7] cannot masquerade as a source.
Embeddings are cached in IndexedDB under a fingerprint of the model and chunk text, so repeat visits skip indexing and any storage failure just means recompute.
Every failure degrades instead of blocking: no key gives extractive cited answers, an API error keeps the retrieved passages on screen, and a failed model download leaves keyword search working.

title: a11y-kit: accessible React components with live axe auditing
tagline: Twelve WAI-ARIA components I hand-built in strict TypeScript, documented in Storybook and audited by axe-core in the page.
summary: A component library implementing Dialog, Tabs, Combobox, Menu, Accordion, Stepper, Toast, Tooltip, Switch, Radio group, a sortable Data table and a skip-link/landmark layout directly from the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, with no UI library behind the behaviour. A playground runs axe-core against the live DOM on every interaction and theme change, and Storybook documents each pattern's keyboard model. I verify behaviour with Vitest and Cypress using real key events.
role: Sole author: component APIs, accessibility behaviour, theming, Storybook docs, tests and tooling
highlights: I wrote the shared primitives (useRovingFocus, useFocusTrap, useInert, useTypeahead, useStableId) with compound-component APIs, composeHandlers overrides and a polymorphic props type under strict TypeScript.
My Stepper's arrow-key order skips unavailable steps and re-derives its single tab stop each render, so locking the focused step cannot strand keyboard users.

The Dialog has a focus trap, inert background, focus return and a document-level Escape stack. Cypress with real Tab events caught a focus-return failure (restoring focus while still inert) that jsdom could not.
I built the Toast system on persistent polite and assertive live regions with hover- and focus-pausable timers, and the Tooltip to WCAG 1.4.13.
Light, dark and high-contrast themes come from CSS variables only, with prefers-reduced-motion handled through one duration token.
The playground audit panel runs axe-core live: 0 violations at rest and in 24 theme-by-open-state combinations, with nothing suppressed.

title: Pipeline — 50,000-deal sales table
tagline: A keyboard-first, virtualized CRM table that stays smooth on an unreliable network.
summary: A frontend I built for a shared 50,000-deal pipeline used by about 20 reps. A fake API simulates latency, save failures and teammates editing the same deals. The UI uses optimistic, queued saves with per-row status and per-row failure recovery.
highlights: A virtualized table (TanStack Virtual) renders all 50,000 deals, with client-side filter, sort, multi-select and bulk stage moves.
I hand-rolled the store on useSyncExternalStore with fine-grained subscriptions, so a single row update does not re-render the table.
Saves are optimistic and queued, with per-row sync indicators and a failed-saves action that shows which rows failed instead of retrying blindly.
I fixed a stale-save race where a slow response overwrote a newer edit on the same deal, and documented it in the write-up.
It is fully keyboard-driven: arrow navigation, shift-range selection, number keys to move stage, and / to search.
State persists to IndexedDB, so reloads resume mid-flight, including failed saves.
